name: Sleep apnea surgery / MMA

lead: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) surgically moves the upper and lower jaws forward, enlarging the airway behind the tongue. It is described as one of the most effective surgical treatments for sleep apnea, and appearance communities discuss it for the more forward jaw and more defined profile that result.

Advancing the jaws pulls attached tissues forward and widens the airway. The skeletal change is plainly measurable. The technique, also called bimaxillary advancement or orthognathic surgery, was first used to correct facial skeletal deformities and malocclusion; from the late 1970s lower jaw advancement was noted to improve sleepiness in patients.

paras: It is performed by oral and maxillofacial surgeons, often with genioglossus advancement, and is usually considered after other treatments such as nasal surgery or tonsillectomy have not worked. Planning typically involves imaging and dental or orthodontic work. Registered trials are ongoing, including comparisons of splintless versus conventional MMA.

It is major surgery. Recovery is longer than for other sleep apnea surgeries because the facial bones must heal in their new position. Specific risk details were not provided in the sources reviewed, so candidates discuss them with a surgeon.

angle.text: MMA moves the upper and lower jaws forward to open the airway, and the skeletal change is visible in the facial profile. It is described as among the most effective sleep apnea surgeries and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for the jaw projection it produces.

lead: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA), also called bimaxillary advancement or orthognathic surgery, moves the upper and lower jaws forward. [1] It was first used to correct facial skeletal deformities and malocclusion, and from the late 1970s advancing the lower jaw was noted to improve sleepiness in patients. [1]

It is described as one of the most effective surgical treatments for obstructive sleep apnea, often done with genioglossus advancement and usually after other treatments fail. [1] Recovery is longer than for other sleep surgeries. [1]
Registered trials are ongoing or planned, including comparisons of splintless versus conventional MMA. [2][3][4]

paras: MMA advances the upper and lower jaws together, and is classed as a sleep surgery. [1] It is usually considered after nasal surgery, tonsillectomy, uvulopalatopharyngoplasty or tongue reduction have not worked. [1]

Registered trials include a planned 66-person trial comparing splintless with conventional MMA for obstructive sleep apnea, an 80-person trial of MMA in OSA begun in 2018 whose status is unknown, and an 80-person quality-of-life study of MMA patients begun in 2023. [2][3][4] No results from these registrations were retrieved.

timeline.event: Registration of an 80-patient MMA trial for OSA begins. [3]
